title: Thread Implementation Models
summary: How application-level threads actually map onto kernel-schedulable entities — user-level, kernel-level, and hybrid models, and why every mainstream OS ended up at one-to-one.

slides.markdown:
"A thread" isn't one fixed thing — it depends on **who's doing the scheduling**. A thread your code creates could be a lightweight userspace bookkeeping trick the kernel never even sees, or a fully kernel-visible entity the OS scheduler treats just like a process.

The mapping between the two is called the **threading model**: many-to-one, one-to-one, or many-to-many. This sounds academic, but it directly answers a real interview question — "why did one blocking system call freeze my entire multi-threaded program?" — which only makes sense once you know which model is in play.

slides.sectionTitle: User-level threads: managed entirely in userspace
slides.markdown:
**User-level threads** are created, scheduled, and switched entirely by a library running in your application's own address space — the kernel has no idea they exist at all. It sees one single process (and, in the many-to-one model below, one single kernel thread).

The upside: creating and switching between user-level threads never crosses into the kernel, so it's extremely fast — no syscall, no kernel scheduler involvement, just the userspace library saving a few registers and jumping to a different stack.

The catch, covered on the next slides, is that the kernel schedules what it can see — and if it can't see your threads, it can only schedule (or block) the one thing it does see: the process as a whole.

slides.sectionTitle: Kernel-level threads: the OS schedules each one
slides.markdown:
**Kernel-level threads** are created and scheduled by the OS kernel itself — each one has its own kernel data structure (its own entry the scheduler can see and dispatch independently), the same way a process does.

The upside: if one kernel thread blocks on a syscall (disk read, network I/O), the kernel simply schedules a different kernel thread from the same or a different process onto the core — nothing else in that process needs to stop. The cost: creating one and switching to it goes through the kernel, which is slower than a pure userspace switch (though still far cheaper than a full process context switch, since the address space doesn't change).

This is the model Linux and Windows actually use for their default threads — see the one-to-one slide.

slides.sectionTitle: Many-to-one model and its blocking problem
slides.markdown:
In **many-to-one**, many user-level threads map onto a single kernel thread — the kernel sees exactly one schedulable entity no matter how many threads your program thinks it has. Thread creation and switching are extremely fast (all in userspace), but there's a fatal flaw: if *any one* of those user-level threads makes a blocking system call, the single underlying kernel thread blocks — and since the kernel doesn't know the other user-level threads even exist, **all of them freeze**, even though most were ready to run.

This was a real design used by early threading libraries (pre-NPTL Linux pthreads, old Solaris green threads), and it's exactly why it fell out of favor once multi-core machines became standard — many-to-one also can't use more than one CPU core, since the kernel only ever sees one schedulable thing per process.

slides.sectionTitle: One-to-one model — what Linux/Windows actually use
slides.markdown:
In **one-to-one**, every user-visible thread maps to exactly one kernel thread, one-for-one. When you call `pthread_create()` on Linux, you get a real kernel-scheduled entity (Linux calls it a task, same underlying structure as a process, just sharing the address space) — the kernel can schedule it on any core, and if it blocks, every other thread keeps running untouched.

The trade-off is the mirror image of many-to-one: thread creation and context switches now cost a syscall each, which is slower than a pure-userspace switch, but you get real multi-core parallelism and no all-or-nothing blocking. This trade won decisively as multi-core hardware became the norm — the one blocking call freezing everything became unacceptable, and the per-thread syscall overhead became cheap by comparison to what you'd lose otherwise.

**Many-to-many** tries to get the best of both: many user-level threads are multiplexed onto a smaller (but more than one) pool of kernel threads. The runtime can create as many lightweight user-level threads as it wants without a kernel thread for each one, while still spreading them across multiple kernel threads so one blocking call doesn't freeze everything — only whichever kernel thread that call happened to be riding on.

A **two-level model** is a many-to-many variant that also allows specific user-level threads to be permanently bound one-to-one to their own kernel thread, for cases needing a guarantee that thread won't be affected by another thread's blocking.

In practice, many-to-many needs a genuinely sophisticated runtime scheduler to pull off well, which is a large part of why most general-purpose OSes settled on the simpler one-to-one model instead.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: the three threading models side by side
slides.markdown:
![Many-to-one, one-to-one, and many-to-many thread models](assets/thread-models.svg)

The number of lines converging into each kernel square is the whole story: many-to-one has one square doing all the work (and one blocking call stops it entirely), one-to-one has a dedicated square per circle (maximum isolation, maximum syscall cost), and many-to-many sits in between, trading some isolation for fewer kernel threads than user threads.

slides.sectionTitle: Green threads / userland schedulers as a modern many-to-one variant
slides.markdown:
Many-to-one didn't disappear — it came back in a smarter form. **Green threads** and userland schedulers (Go's goroutines, Erlang's processes, older Java green threads) are user-level threads managed by a language runtime, but the modern versions fix the original blocking flaw by combining many-to-many underneath: the runtime multiplexes many green threads over a small pool of real OS (kernel) threads, and when a green thread would block on I/O, the runtime intercepts it and parks just that one green thread while moving the OS thread on to run a different green thread.

Go's goroutines are the clearest interview-relevant example: you can spawn hundreds of thousands of them cheaply (a few KB of stack each, growable, versus a few MB for an OS thread), and the Go runtime's scheduler (`GOMAXPROCS` OS threads underneath) handles the many-to-many multiplexing so a blocking network call doesn't stall unrelated goroutines.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: user-level vs kernel-level — cost, blocking, scheduler control
slides.markdown:
| | User-level threads | Kernel-level threads |
|---|---|---|
| Creation/switch cost | Very cheap — no syscall | More expensive — goes through the kernel |
| Blocking behavior | One blocking call can freeze others (many-to-one) unless the runtime handles it | Blocking one thread never affects others |
| Multi-core use | Only with a many-to-many/hybrid runtime | Native — kernel freely schedules across cores |
| Scheduler control | Application/runtime controls scheduling policy | OS scheduler controls it, less app control |
| Visibility to OS tools | Often invisible to `ps`/`top` (one process entry) | Each thread visible individually |

**How to decide:** if you need maximal control over scheduling and extremely high thread counts with I/O-heavy blocking patterns, a well-built many-to-many runtime (Go, Erlang) wins; for most general-purpose application code, the OS's native one-to-one threads are the simpler, safer default.
